## About this report

This is a Quarto document. Its R code sits in chunks, the shaded blocks
below. Run a chunk with the button on its header, or render the whole
report with Render above the document. The finished report opens beside
the code.

On a clear night away from city lights, a few thousand stars are in
view. From a town, it is closer to nine hundred. This report looks at
those nine hundred: how far away they are, why they differ in color, and
which of them are giants.

## The stars you can see

```{r}
stars <- read.csv("data/bright_stars.csv")
nrow(stars)
summary(stars$distance_ly)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
near <- sum(stars$distance_ly < 100)
far <- sum(stars$distance_ly > 1000)
```

Only `r near` of them are within 100 light years. `r far` are more than
1,000 light years away, so the light reaching Earth from them left before the
first printed book.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "The whole sky, flattened. Brighter stars are drawn larger, in their own colors."
par(bg = "#0B1020", fg = "#8A93A8", col.axis = "#8A93A8", col.lab = "#C9D1E0", mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(dec_degrees ~ ra_hours, data = stars, pch = 16, col = stars$color,
     cex = 0.25 + (4.6 - stars$magnitude) * 0.42, xlim = c(24, 0), ylim = c(-90, 90),
     xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", xlab = "Right ascension, hours", ylab = "Declination, degrees")
brightest <- subset(stars, magnitude < 1)
text(brightest$ra_hours, brightest$dec_degrees, brightest$name, pos = 3, cex = 0.6, col = "#C9D1E0")
```

## Why stars differ in color

A star's color is its temperature. The hottest burn blue-white and the
coolest glow orange.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "How many bright stars there are at each temperature, each bar in the color of that temperature."
bands <- cut(stars$temperature_k, breaks = seq(2000, 32000, by = 1000))
counts <- table(bands)
middle <- seq(2500, 31500, by = 1000)
shade <- stars$color[sapply(middle, function(t) which.min(abs(stars$temperature_k - t)))]
par(bg = "#0B1020", fg = "#8A93A8", col.axis = "#8A93A8", col.lab = "#C9D1E0", mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
barplot(counts[counts > 0], col = shade[counts > 0], border = NA, las = 2,
        names.arg = format(middle[counts > 0], big.mark = ","), ylab = "Stars", cex.names = 0.7)
```

## Giants and ordinary stars

```{r}
table(stars$kind)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
giants <- subset(stars, kind %in% c("giant", "supergiant"))
share <- round(100 * nrow(giants) / nrow(stars))
```

Most stars in the galaxy are small and dim, yet `r share` percent of the
stars bright enough to see from a town are giants or supergiants. They
shine so strongly that they can be seen from far away, while ordinary stars
at the same distance are too faint for the eye.

## The closest bright stars

```{r}
closest <- stars[order(stars$distance_ly), c("name", "constellation", "distance_ly", "kind")]
head(closest, 8)
```

The star data comes from the HYG Database, version 4.1, by David Nash,

is worked out from each star's color index (Ballesteros 2012).
